El resumen va en español, en 2-3 frases, escrito por ti a partir del cuerpo que devolvió `wine_article_fetch`. content.text: The news is about Quilceda Creek, a Washington winery. Let me fetch the article to see what it's about. Quilceda Creek is a famous Washington State Cabernet Sauvignon producer. Let me read the article.
He recibido la noticia sobre Quilceda Creek (Washington). Ahora leo el artículo completo para poder resumir con material real.

Quilceda Creek: The Remix

Artículo completo (6000 caracteres, recortado):

Here is my confession: I disrespected two of the most acclaimed, hard-to-get wines from the Pacific Northwest. The winery might be angry at me. But I have no regrets, because it worked, the result was delicious, and I spent the weekend drinking terrific Cabernets that nobody can replicate. I had a 192-point weekend. Related stories: Saving Washington's Wine Industry Washington Wine Takes Another Blow Napa Winemakers' Call of the Wild I do not blend wines; i.e., pour two different wines together into the same glass. It's disrespectful. I once yelled at my friend Steve for combining two Uruguayan Tannats I brought to his house for a party at which he cooked me dinner. Steve! Don't do that! One at a time! So here is the tale of how I came to do this with two single-vineyard wines from what may be Washington 's greatest winery, Quilceda Creek . In a state where the wine industry has been reeling since the downfall of Chateau Ste Michelle, Quilceda Creek is a success story. The winery has been buying up vineyards and just this month acquired 100 percent of Champoux Vineyard, which has some of the state's oldest Cabernet Sauvignon vines. We at Wine-Searcher were overdue to check in on Quilceda Creek, because many of you love their wines. Quilceda Creek makes 12,000 cases per year, and only 1000 cases of one wine go to restaurants and retail stores; the rest is sold direct to mailing list members. But Quilceda Creek is more searched by our readers than Robert Mondavi Winery or The Prisoner or Duckhorn or ... I could go on. And no wonder. Quilceda Creek is a critics' darling, with four 100-point scores from Wine Advocate , five 99s and 15 98s. But that's not owner/winemaker Paul Golitizin's goal. "Our wines are like riper Bordeaux , but with more consistency," Paul Golitzin told Wine-Searcher. "I want people to catch onto that. I want people to drink a glass and say, 'I want another glass.'" For a winery with its reputation, the wines are fairly priced. There are four official current releases, all officially $250 if you can get them, but they're sold at lower prices to their mailing list so you can often find them cheaper on our site. I know, $250 isn't cheap, but if you compare it to wines of Napa or Bordeaux that get similar ratings, it kinda is. "We think compared to wines that are $450 to $500, those wines are not as pure," said general manager Scott Lloyd, who is from Napa Valley. "We're getting the word out that Quilceda Creek is world-class Cabernet . Once people learn that, they wonder, why am I paying those (higher) prices?" So I was happy to visit the residential neighborhood north of Seattle that has grown up around the winery, which was in the middle of a forest when Alex Golitzin founded it. His son Paul runs the show now and is a low-key, fun-loving horror movie fan who, I was warned, doesn't like talking about making wine because he doesn't like to talk about himself. Well, I like horror movies, I can work with that. (His favorite is John Carpenter's "The Thing" and he and I are among the few Americans to have seen and loved the Norwegian prequel.) Maybe humility is a natural result of descending from pre-revolution Russian royalty. One of Paul's ancestors, Prince Lev Sergeyevich, was winemaker for Czar Nicholas II. Another, Prince Nikolay Dmitriyevich, was the last prime minister of Czarist Russia . Other relatives include an Olympic gold-medal diver, a movie art director who won three Oscars, a physicist noted for research into the concept of nuclear winter, the inventor of the first electromagnetic seismograph, and a general who governed Moscow for 25 years. Against that backdrop, perhaps "serial creator of 99-point wines" isn't something he feels he can brag about. In fact, two of the library wines Paul poured on my visit were 100-pointers, a fact I discovered only when I got home. I haven't yet been to a Napa Valley winery where those scores wouldn't have been mentioned. Paul's father Alex is a retired chemical engineer whose cousin Andre Tchelistcheff, the most important winemaker in California history, sponsored his family to move to the United States. Alex founded Quilceda Creek in the 1970s because he said there was nothing good to drink in Washington, where he was working at a big paper company. Tchelitscheff, who consulted for many of California's best wineries in the 1970s and '80s, said he would teach Alex to make wine, and he did. Alex made his first commercial vintage in his garage in 1979; Quilceda Creek became one of 12 wineries in the state (there are now more than 900). Unlike his dad, Paul grew up in the winery. His father brought him along on a visit to Andre Lurton in Bordeaux. Paul was just 15 and the lunch stretched on forever, as French countryside lunches do. Alex thought Paul would be bored, but instead, Paul told him that he decided that day that wine was what he wanted to do for the rest of his life. "My dad says I was blotto," Paul says, "but I think he was." Drinking Bordeaux all day: I'm sure they were both right. Alex put Paul in charge of winemaking in 1994, and accolades have rolled in ever since. Don't let Paul's casual nature fool you: there's fastidiousness and precision to everything Quilceda Creek does. It may have started because of Alex's engineering background, but it continues today with his Hawaiian-shirt wearing son. #img2# For example, in 2010 Quilceda Creek finally got the opportunity to move winemaking out of what had been a house when a neighbor agreed to sell her property. Alex had years to rue not buying more of the surrounding forest as it was chopped down for housing that hemmed in his business. With a new lot next door, the engineer could design and build the perfect gravity-flow winery; that's what I expected. Instead, they built a big empty two-room building that looks like an airplane hangar. Why? The answer is flexibility to make as many small lots of wine as they want. Quilceda Creek makes almost all of its wine in stain

Now I have the full article. Let me summarize the key points:

- The article is about Quilceda Creek, a winery in Washington state (Pacific Northwest, USA)
- The writer confesses to blending two single-vineyard wines from Quilceda Creek, which is a critics' darling with four 100-point scores from Wine Advocate
- Quilceda Creek makes world-class Cabernet Sauvignon, described as "riper Bordeaux"
- They just acquired 100% of Champoux Vineyard, with some of the state's oldest Cabernet Sauvignon vines
- The wines are Cabernet-based, Washington state, compared to Bordeaux

Now, which wine in the store connects? Looking at the stock:
- SKU-1001 | Tenuta San Guido Sassicaia (tinto, Bolgheri, Toscana, Italia, Cabernet Sauvignon / Cabernet Franc) | 189€ — Sassicaia is a Cabernet Sauvignon-based blend, often compared to Bordeaux. Connection: Cabernet Sauvignon, "riper Bordeaux" style.
- SKU-1002 | Vega Sicilia Único (Tempranillo / Cabernet Sauvignon) — includes Cabernet Sauvignon, Ribera del Duero
- SKU-1005 | Penfolds Grange (Shiraz) — no

The strongest connection: Quilceda Creek is a Cabernet Sauvignon blend (with Cabernet Franc) styled after "riper Bordeaux". Sassicaia is a Cabernet Sauvignon/Cabernet Franc blend from Bolgheri, also Bordeaux-inspired (the "super Tuscan" born from Bordeaux grapes). That's a real, meaningful connection: both are Cabernet Sauvignon-dominant blends inspired by Bordeaux, with Cabernet Franc as the second variety. Also Quilceda Creek's wines are described as "riper Bordeaux" — Sassicaia is literally called "the first super Tuscan" made from Bordeaux varieties.

Vega Sicilia Único is also a blend of Tempranillo/Cabernet Sauvignon but Tempranillo-dominant, less close.

So I'll recommend SKU-1001 Sassicaia. Motivo: la noticia celebra Quilceda Creek como Cabernet Sauvignon de clase mundial, estilo "Burdeos más maduro"; Sassicaia es un blend de Cabernet Sauvignon/Cabernet Franc nacido en Bolgheri como homenaje al Burdeos, la misma filosofía de blend bordelés con uvas cabernet.
